record.title: Subject-dependent, subject-independent, or pooled? What each evaluation regime really measures in EEG imagined-speech decoding
record.abstract: Reported accuracies for EEG imagined-speech decoding vary widely and are difficult to compare, partly because studies differ in the evaluation regime they use. We examine what published "within-subject" results on the five-class imagined-speech track of the 2020 International BCI Competition (BCIC2020-3; 15 subjects, 64 channels) actually measure. Using a compact topographic-map convolutional network as a fixed measurement instrument, we apply an identical held-out test set across three training regimes: subject-dependent (SD), subject-independent leave-one-subject-out (SI), and pooled (subject-mixed). SD decoding reaches 49.7% balanced accuracy; SI decoding is near chance (22.5%); pooled evaluation reaches 41.1%. Because the pooled and SI models differ only in whether the target subject appeared in training, the 18.5 percentage-point gap between them measures subject-specific information that does not transfer to an unseen user. A protocol triangulation with a predefined leakage control further shows that shuffled cross-validation can inflate an individual subject by up to 24.6 points. The dataset nonetheless contains genuine subject-dependent signal, remaining well above chance under a leakage-safe protocol. We conclude that "within-subject" benchmarks on this dataset are subject-mixed and partly inflated, and that imagined-speech accuracy should be reported by explicit regime.
